newsitem.title: UK: IRA bomb victim dies, raising N.Ireland tension.
newsitem.headline: IRA bomb victim dies, raising N.Ireland tension.

text.p: A British soldier caught in the first IRA bombing in Northern Ireland for over two years died of his injuries on Friday, bringing down fresh condemnation on the republican guerrillas and their political allies.

Warrant Officer James Bradwell, 43, was the first British soldier to die on active duty in Northern Ireland since the Irish Republican Army (IRA) and its Protestant Loyalist rivals called ceasefires in 1994
The IRA called off its ceasefire in February, but had since then targetted English cities.

The father-of-three had suffered 60 percent burns in the double car bombing at the British Army's headquarters in Northern Ireland at Lisburn, 10 miles (15 km) from Belfast. He was one of 31 people injured.
Told of Bradwell's death, British Prime Minister John Major launched an emotional attack on Gerry Adams, leader of the IRA"s political wing, Sinn Fein.
"Don't tell me this has nothing to do with you. I don't believe you, Mr Adams, I don't believe you," Major said in his keynote speech to the annual Conservative Party conference.

"He (Bradwell) was murdered in cold blood in the United Kingdom. I sent him there, Mr Adams, so spare me any crocodile tears." Major said the bombing had damaged Sinn Fein's chances of being allowed into peace talks.

"Bombs will not bring Sinn Fein into the talks. All they mean is that Sinn Fein has slammed the door on themselves," Major told his Conservative Party's annual conference in Bournemouth, southern England.
Sinn Fein has been barred from joining the talks, sponsored by Britain and Ireland, until the IRA calls a new truce.
Major said he was still adamant that IRA weapons must be decommissioned and said his government would introduce new laws setting out how the weapons could be disposed of.
"I want those weapons off the street," Major said.
Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, who this week accused the IRA of using Nazi tactics, also said violence would not help the republicans' campaign for a united Ireland.

"Others in politics do not reserve to themselves the option of going back to violence, or support for violence, if political developments do not match their aims. Sinn Fein cannot expect to be an exception to that rule," Bruton said in a statement.

Bradwell's death came as the IRA's pro-British Loyalist rivals contemplated their response to the Lisburn bombing, which some fear will lead them to abandon their own ceasefire and reignite Northern Ireland's quarter-century of sectarian war.
Some Loyalist political leaders said Bradwell's death made it more likely the guerrillas would resort to violence.

"It is obviously a tragedy and likely to have a negative response from Loyalists... This is the sort of action that could actually plummet us back into the depths of war, " said Billy Hutchinson of the Progressive Unionist Party, the political arm of the outlawed Ulster Volunteer Force.
"I still insist that Loyalists should remain calm and hold on to the ceasefire," he told Reuters.

There has so far been no public word from the Combioyalist Command (CMLC), which rules over the Protestant guerrilla groups. The CMLC is expected to meet within the next few days and newspapers said the group may issue a response on Sunday, the second anniversary of its ceasefire.

The IRA, which has denied it is trying to provoke the Loyalists into violence, has come under strong pressure to revive the 17-month truce it abandoned on February 9 with the first of a series of bombings on the British mainland.
A poll published on Friday suggested 92 percent of Northern Irish Catholics wanted the IRA to call a new truce.
